report:
### Conclusion
For the general population, **no**—regular intake of vitamin C does not prevent common colds, though it modestly reduces their duration and severity and can prevent colds in specific high-stress groups.

### Evidence Summary
* **General Public (No Prevention):** Systematic reviews and large-scale clinical trials show that routine vitamin C supplementation ($\ge200\text{ mg/day}$) does not reduce the incidence or likelihood of catching a cold in the general public.
* **High Physical Stress (Effective Prevention):** Vitamin C supplementation reduces cold risk by approximately 50% in individuals exposed to short periods of severe physical stress or extreme cold, such as marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers training in subarctic conditions.
* **Duration and Severity:** Although regular intake does not prevent infection in most people, consistent prophylactic supplementation modestly shortens cold duration—by roughly 8% in adults and 14% in children—and can reduce symptom severity. Taking vitamin C only after cold symptoms start shows no consistent benefit.

### Sources
* Cochrane Review: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold
* NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminC-HealthProfessional/
* Linus Pauling Institute: https://lpi.oregonstate.edu/mic/health-disease/common-cold
